content.comment_body: I've been using [product_name] 220V for home automation for 20 years without prior issues. However, in the last 5 years, I've needed to replace the bathroom light relay three times across different modules. Although the bathroom light is used most frequently, my calculations show it's not exceeding 10,000,000 cycles every two years. The light has a maximum of 60W, now replaced with a 12W LED. When problems start, you can temporarily resolve it by resetting or powering off the module, but eventually, the contact gets stuck in the ON position permanently, even after power is off. Upon disassembly, I never found the contact still blocked. Based on my experience, it seems the internal relay quality has decreased noticeably in the past several years. Has anyone else encountered similar issues with these 220V relays?

The issue isn't with the relays themselves, but with the LED lamps. LED lights have a very high inrush current, exceeding what the [product_name] relay can handle. In such cases, it's better to control appropriate contactors instead of relays, as they're designed for high inrush currents. Alternatively, consider using inrush current limiters such as [product_name] ICL230.
You could also look for inrush current limiters like eQ-3 Inrush Current Limiter ESB1.

analysis.insight_summary: Users report failures of relay outputs on [product_name] used for switching LED lamps, especially in applications like bathroom lighting. The fault often appears as relay contacts sticking in the ON position, needing resets or power cycles that only temporarily restore function. Concern has been raised regarding perceived reliability, though community responses suggest high LED inrush current is the main cause, rather than relay quality, and recommend contactors or inrush current limiters as solutions.
analysis.user_expectations: Users expect [product_name] relay outputs to reliably switch LED loads without repeated failures or frequent replacements, even with frequent use.
